questions.question: Oliver, you said something in our chat that stuck with me—that the classroom in Hard Times isn't really about education, it's about killing performance. Can you unpack that? Because I think most people read Gradgrind's opening scene and think: Victorian satire on bad schools. You're saying something weirder and more interesting than that.
questions.intent: Get Oliver's theatrical thesis on the table early—the idea that Gradgrind's classroom and Stephen's stoop are the same suppression of performance. This frames the whole segment and gives Daniel and Edmund something to react to.

questions.question: Daniel, I want to go straight to that passage everyone's been quoting—'In the strength of his misfortune, and the energy of his distress, he fired for a moment like a proud man.' Edmund reads that as Dickens giving us a soul. You read it as something closer to a body under pressure. What do you mean by that?
questions.intent: Get Daniel's materialist/physiological reading of the passage out into the open—dignity as a 'flash' the system crushes back down—so Edmund can push back hard. Sets up the segment's central disagreement.

questions.question: Edmund, I can see you itching to respond. Because if I'm hearing Daniel right, Stephen's dignity isn't really *his*—it's just what a body does under stress before the machine wins. That seems like it guts the whole moral reading of the character. What's wrong with that?
questions.intent: Provoke Edmund's strongest counter—that Stephen is a study in moral heroism, not a physiological specimen—and get him to quote the passage himself. The 'proud man' line and the 'demon in her shape' line should both come out here.

questions.question: Oliver, you want to read that 'bound hand and foot, to a dead woman, and tormented by a demon in her shape' passage aloud—and then I want you to tell me whether you think Dickens is *in control* of that language or whether it's running away from him. Because you said something about melodrama being a feature, not a bug, and I want to understand what that means.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform the passage—good radio moment—and then open the melodrama-vs-genuine-tragedy debate. Edmund will want to defend the Jacobean register; Daniel will want to read it as indictment rather than pathos.

questions.question: Daniel, you said the classroom and the marriage law are the same institution with different walls. That's a big claim. Walk me through it—because to Edmund that probably sounds like you're flattening two completely different kinds of human suffering into one political argument.
questions.intent: Force Daniel to defend his structural thesis directly against Edmund's character-centred reading. This is the segment's climactic cross-engagement—the sharpest ideological disagreement—and should produce the best radio.

steering_notes: The segment has a natural arc: start with Oliver's theatrical framing (unusual, disarming), move into the central passage dispute between Edmund and Daniel, use Oliver as the swing voice who agrees with both and neither. The key tension is Edmund's moral-heroism reading vs Daniel's structural-damage reading—keep returning to the physical text, especially c9:p27 and c10:p35, to anchor the argument. Don't let this become abstract too early. The moment Oliver reads 'bound hand and foot' aloud is the emotional peak—time the melodrama question to land right after that. Watch for Edmund getting defensive when Daniel calls Stephen's dignity 'physiological'—that's the flashpoint. Also watch for Daniel and Oliver accidentally agreeing that the system produces suffering, which leaves Edmund isolated; that's a good late-segment moment to push Edmund to go further on why that reading matters.
cross_engagement_targets: Both Edmund and Daniel want to quote the same passage—'fired for a moment like a proud man'—but mean completely opposite things by it. Let them both claim it before asking who's right.

Oliver thinks the 'demon in her shape' melodrama is intentional characterisation of Stephen's self-pity; Edmund thinks it elevates Stephen to tragic dignity; Daniel thinks it names the marriage law as literal violence. Three readings of one sentence—get all three on the table simultaneously.

Daniel's claim that the classroom and marriage law are 'the same institution' will irritate Edmund, who sees Stephen's moral predicament as irreducibly individual. That's the segment's sharpest disagreement and should be saved for the final third.

Oliver and Daniel actually share more than they admit—both think the system *deforms* people physically and psychologically. Pointing this out will force Edmund to defend his position harder, and might produce an interesting Oliver pivot.

segment_name: The Grinding of Souls: Louisa's Emotional Void

questions.question: Oliver, you've argued that these passages were basically written to be performed — that the real violence is *rhythmic*, something you feel in your throat when you read it aloud. Can you actually do that for us? Take us through that sequence in c13:p49 — the 'You have been so careful of me' passage — and show us what you mean.
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read the anaphoric passage aloud, demonstrating the funeral-bell rhythm, which then gives Rosen and Leigh something concrete and visceral to respond to and interpret differently

questions.question: Daniel, you've said Louisa isn't broken — she's *optimised*. That she will marry Bounderby and be an excellent rational wife and that's the actual horror. But Edmund's going to tell us this is a story about one man's moral failure, not a system. So which is it — is Gradgrind a villain-of-capitalism type, or is he just a particular father who got something catastrophically wrong about love?
questions.intent: Force the direct Leigh vs Rosen disagreement about whether the tragedy is personal or structural — this is their core clash and the segment's central tension

questions.question: Edmund, you want to quote Louisa asking 'What do I know, father, of tastes and fancies' — and you've called that existential grief rather than political anger. But Daniel would say that her *not knowing* is the whole point: Gradgrind has colonised her interior life so completely she can't even name what was stolen. She's thanking him for the theft. Doesn't that actually make it *more* political, not less?
questions.intent: Push Leigh on his personal-tragedy reading using Rosen's 'ideology speaks in the voice of protection' argument — see if Leigh concedes anything or doubles down

questions.question: Oliver, you've flagged that scene in c13:p21 where Gradgrind basically demonstrates marriage to Louisa like a logical proof — 'Does Mr. Bounderby ask me to marry him? Yes, he does.' You said it's almost farcical, that Dickens wants us to *laugh* at him. But are we really laughing? Because that trap snapping shut on a teenage girl feels to me less like comedy and more like — I don't know — something much darker.
questions.intent: Draw out the tension between Trevelyan's performative/comedic reading and the genuine horror of the scene — invite Rosen especially to respond on the ideological mechanics of that 'logical trap'

questions.question: Edmund, you want to use that Time's factory passage — c12:p51, 'his Hands are mutes' — to argue the factory isn't the villain, that the grinding comes from within. But Oliver reads 'Hands' as Dickens winking at his own industrial critique, and Daniel reads the whole image as Dickens showing that the *system* is the thing doing the grinding, not any individual. So when Dickens reaches for factory language to describe a human soul — what's he actually telling us?
questions.intent: Use the single shared passage (c12:p51) that all three experts want to quote, but for completely different purposes, as a flashpoint — let each of them fight over what Dickens meant by it

steering_notes: The segment's richest tension is Leigh vs Rosen on personal vs structural tragedy — keep returning to that fault line. Let Trevelyan's performative energy be the warm entry point (get the reading aloud early) but make sure his comedic reading of Gradgrind gets properly challenged, because the other two will both resist it. The c12:p51 'Hands are mutes' passage is the ideal flashpoint because all three experts cite it for contradictory purposes — save it for late in the segment when they're warmed up enough to really argue. Watch for Rosen wanting to pivot to Sparsit as a parallel case — that's a good thread but don't let it derail the Louisa focus. If energy dips, push anyone to read a passage aloud.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh argues Gradgrind is a particular man with a moral failure; Rosen argues he is a functional component of a system — this is the segment's spine and should be surfaced early and returned to

Trevelyan reads the 'You have been so careful' anaphora as theatrical crescendo and a form of power Dickens gives Louisa; Rosen reads the same passage as evidence that ideology speaks in the voice of protection and Louisa cannot hear her own dispossession — direct contradiction worth staging explicitly

All three experts want to quote c12:p51 (Time's factory / 'Hands are mutes') but for entirely different purposes: Leigh uses it to say the factory is not the villain; Trevelyan uses it as evidence of Dickens's linguistic playfulness; Rosen uses it as structural critique. Put all three readings on the table simultaneously.

Trevelyan's insistence on the comedy of c13:p21 (Gradgrind's logical trap) sits in direct tension with Rosen's reading of the same passage as ideological violence dressed as rationality — worth a direct 'Oliver, Daniel sees nothing funny there' prompt

segment_name: System and Suffering: Stephen's Impossible Choice

questions.question: Oliver, you've said that Stephen's appeal to Bounderby is structured like a barrister's argument — that he's not pleading, he's *prosecuting*. Can you read us the passage and make that case? Because I think a lot of readers hear the dialect and assume pathos, not rhetoric.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read c9:p51 and establish the 'eloquence as power' reading early — this directly sets up the disagreement with Edmund about whether Stephen is constrained by inner scrupulousness or defeated from without

questions.question: Daniel, you'd push back on the word 'eloquence' entirely, wouldn't you? Because your argument is that it doesn't matter how brilliantly Stephen speaks — Bounderby's line, 'the institutions of your country are not your piece-work', is basically telling him he doesn't have the *right* to diagnose his own situation. That's a different kind of trap than just not being heard.
questions.intent: Draw out Daniel's sharpest systemic reading and get him to quote c9:p61 — the 'piece-work' line — so we can contrast it with Oliver's framing of eloquence as meaningful resistance

questions.question: Edmund, I want to put something uncomfortable to you. Both Oliver and Daniel are essentially arguing about *external* forces — the rhetoric, the legal machinery, the class power. But you've said Stephen's real torment is *internal*, that his scrupulousness is itself a kind of trap. Isn't that dangerously close to saying he does this to himself?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to articulate and defend his 'moral paralysis' reading against the implicit charge that it lets the system off the hook — this is the sharpest cross-engagement point between Edmund and Daniel

questions.question: Oliver, you've described the Bounderby portrait moment — 'swelling at his own portrait on the wall, as if he were going to explode himself into it' — as Dickens *entertaining himself* while a good man walks into ruin. Edmund thinks it's character comedy. Daniel thinks it's class anatomy. Are any of you actually disagreeing, or are you all just describing different rooms of the same building?
questions.intent: Create a moment of productive synthesis or sharper disagreement — push all three to clarify what's actually at stake in how we read Bounderby, and whether 'farce', 'moral failure', and 'systemic cruelty' are compatible or competing readings

questions.question: Daniel, you want to bring in Bitzer — the boy who's become the system's perfect product, calculating even his own refusal to be corrupt. Does that change anything about how we read Stephen? Because Stephen and Bitzer seem to be the same system producing opposite human results, and I'm not sure Dickens thinks one of them chose better than the other.
questions.intent: Introduce the Bitzer contrast to complicate Daniel's systemic reading and invite Edmund and Oliver to weigh in on whether Dickens is ultimately a moralist or a structuralist — the novel's deepest tension

steering_notes: The central fault line is between Edmund's moral-interior reading and Daniel's structural-systemic one, with Oliver occupying interesting middle ground — he believes in Stephen's eloquence and agency while also insisting the system refuses to hear it. Push Edmund and Daniel to talk *to* each other rather than past each other. The best radio moment will come if Edmund concedes the system is cruel but insists Dickens cares more about souls than structures, and Daniel says that's a comforting lie Dickens doesn't actually tell. Oliver should be used as the tiebreaker who reads the prose closely and asks both of them to account for the comedy — because the Bounderby portrait sentence is doing something neither pure moral reading nor pure systemic reading fully explains.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund says Stephen's scrupulousness binds him as much as the law — Daniel will reject this as victim-blaming the conscience; push them to argue it out directly

Oliver reads Stephen's dialect as rhetorical power; Edmund reads the grammar 'breaking under emotion' as Dickens's genius — they're describing the same sentence with opposite conclusions about agency, which is a great radio moment

Daniel's 'piece-work' quote and Edmund's same quote from Bounderby are being used to make completely different arguments — one about class power foreclosing dissent, one about human self-deception. Name this explicitly and ask them to sort it out.
All three want to quote the 'blood upon this land' passage but for different reasons — let Oliver read it, then ask Edmund and Daniel whether they heard the same thing he did

segment_name: Dickens at Play: Wit and Grotesque Comedy

questions.question: Oliver, you've said that Hard Times is actually Dickens at his most entertainingly grotesque — which cuts against how most people read this novel. So let's start there. If you were going to perform a single passage to prove that, what would you pick, and why does it need to be heard rather than read?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform or quote closely from c3:p11 — the 'metallurgical Louisa' passage — and establish the 'performance as meaning' thesis early so the others can push back on it

questions.question: Daniel, you've called these adjectives — 'metallurgical Louisa,' 'mathematical Thomas' — a diagnosis, not just a joke. Edmund is going to say they're a moral observation about Gradgrind's blindness. You're going to say something harder than that. What is it?
questions.intent: Force the Rosen vs. Leigh disagreement into the open early — is the comedy revealing individual moral failure or systemic deformation? Use c3:p11 as the battleground

questions.question: Edmund, you've said that when Mrs. Sparsit is standing there drenched and ruined at the end of chapter twenty-one, that's not Dickens mocking the middle classes — that's the wages of pride. But Daniel is sitting there thinking that's a very comfortable reading, that you're letting the system off the hook. How do you respond to that?
questions.intent: Pit Leigh's 'Christian humiliation' reading directly against Rosen's 'systemic critique' reading of c21:p100 — the Sparsit grotesque as either individual moral lesson or institutional collapse

questions.question: Let's go to Slackbridge — because all three of you want that passage, which tells me something interesting is going on there. Oliver, you've said that when you perform those lines — 'a thief! A plunderer! A proscribed fugitive!' — the emptiness becomes audible. But is Dickens being fair there? Or is the comedy doing something a bit ugly — turning a union organiser into a windbag so we don't have to take him seriously?
questions.intent: Open the question of whether Dickens's comic deflation of Slackbridge is aesthetically brilliant or politically evasive — this should provoke Rosen most strongly, with Leigh having an unexpected alliance with Trevelyan here

questions.question: Edmund, you want to read Stephen's nightmare in chapter eleven as theological — a man's conscience attacking him, not capitalism attacking him. But that passage is extraordinary language, almost Jacobean, 'the millions that were fastened on his face.' Doesn't the sheer excess of that imagery pull against your reading? If it's just about personal guilt, why does Dickens need all those millions?
questions.intent: Press Leigh on the tension between his individualist-moral reading and the social scale of Stephen's nightmare — Trevelyan and Rosen should both want to jump in from very different directions

steering_notes: The segment has a natural arc: start with the comedy-as-performance question (Trevelyan's home turf), move to the ideological fault line over what the grotesque is actually doing (Leigh vs. Rosen), and end on Stephen's nightmare, which is the passage where the comedy cracks and all three readings become most unstable. Keep pushing on specific word choices — 'metallurgical,' 'mathematical,' 'fester' — because that's where the argument lives. If the conversation goes abstract, bring it back to the text. Watch for the moment Leigh and Rosen come closest to agreement (the humanity of Mrs. Sparsit) and use Trevelyan to complicate it.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh's 'wages of pride' reading of Mrs. Sparsit directly conflicts with Rosen's 'institutional fantasy dissolving into mud' reading — they're looking at the same passage and seeing opposite moral directions; push them to name exactly where they diverge

Trevelyan and Rosen are surprisingly close on Slackbridge — both read him as hollow performance — but for completely different reasons (aesthetic vs. political). The question is whether that shared reading of the passage papers over a deep disagreement about what the hollowness means

Leigh's claim that Stephen's nightmare is about personal conscience rather than social victimhood is the sharpest disagreement in the room — both Trevelyan ('performed interiority') and Rosen ('the system's product') will resist it, but from angles that don't agree with each other either. That three-way tension is the most productive moment in the segment

questions.question: Daniel, you've said Gradgrind's pain at the end isn't redemption — it's just the cost of running the machine. But Dickens seems to want us to feel something for him. Is Dickens being naive, or is he deliberately letting Gradgrind off the hook?
questions.intent: Get Rosen's sharpest systemic critique on the table early, and set up Leigh's counter-reading of genuine moral conversion

questions.question: Edmund, I want to push you on Stephen's wife — that passage in c8:p34, 'a creature so foul to look at... but so much fouler than that in her moral infamy.' You read that as Dickens holding her morally accountable, a person whose will has failed. Daniel's going to say Dickens is indicting the system that made her. How do you defend reading moral agency into someone this ground down?
questions.intent: Force the sharpest direct clash between Leigh's moral-portrait reading and Rosen's structural critique, using the same passage both quoted

questions.question: Oliver, you've said facts versus feeling is the stated problem but Dickens solves it through performance — making the facts *sing*. I want you to actually do that with Louisa's confession in c21:p130, that 'I took him. I never made a pretence to him or you that I loved him.' Because Edmund hears moral honesty in that line and Daniel hears emotional amputation. What do you hear when you perform it?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read the passage aloud, demonstrate his performance thesis in practice, and create a moment where the two competing interpretations collide on a single line

questions.question: Edmund, Daniel has argued that Gradgrind never actually values feeling — he just transfers his faith from facts to sentiment and carries on instrumentalizing people. Does Gradgrind's awakening change anything for Louisa or Stephen? Or is Daniel right that the ruling class always finds a way to absorb the cost?
questions.intent: Pressure Leigh's conversion reading against Rosen's structural critique and get Leigh to either defend or qualify Gradgrind's transformation concretely

questions.question: Oliver, Bitzer — c25:p144, 'as if he ran himself into a white heat, when other people ran themselves into a glow.' You called that pure Dickens performance. But Daniel reads Bitzer as the system's perfect product, and Edmund reads him as a horror story about educating the passions out of someone. Can all three readings be true at once, or does the performance reading actually let Dickens off the hook for creating him?
questions.intent: Use the Bitzer passage to triangulate all three interpretations and force a conversation about whether Dickens's comic craft is a moral evasion or a moral instrument

steering_notes: The core tension here is threefold and productive: Leigh wants spiritual conversion, Rosen wants structural critique, Trevelyan wants to dissolve the binary through performance. Don't let Trevelyan's aesthetic reading become a safe third position — push him on whether 'making facts sing' is a political stance or an evasion of one. The Louisa confession passage (c21:p130) and the Stephen's wife description (c8:p34) are the live wires — both Leigh and Rosen quoted the same lines for opposite purposes, which is gold. Get them talking *to* each other about those lines, not past each other. If the conversation gets too abstract, drag it back to the text: 'What does the line actually say?' Keep the energy warm but let disagreements breathe — don't rush to synthesis.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh and Rosen quoted 'so much fouler than that in her moral infamy' for diametrically opposite readings — moral agency vs systemic indictment. This is the sharpest direct clash in the segment and should be surfaced explicitly.

Rosen's claim that Gradgrind 'transfers faith from facts to sentiment' without genuine transformation directly contradicts Leigh's spiritual conversion reading — press both of them on what evidence from the text would settle this.

Trevelyan's performance thesis (facts made to sing) is implicitly a response to both Leigh and Rosen: it sidesteps the moral vs structural debate by relocating Dickens's meaning in craft. Rosen in particular may resist this — flag the tension between aesthetic redemption and political evasion.

All three experts quoted the Bitzer 'white heat' line but with different emphases: Trevelyan on rhythm and comic performance, Leigh on moral horror, Rosen on systemic product. This convergence on a single passage from three angles is a natural moment for a three-way exchange.

questions.question: Oliver, you've said this novel works in the ear before it works in the mind — and I want to test that straight away. That line about M'Choakumchild and the pianoforte legs — can you actually read it for us, and then tell me: what does Dickens *do* with the rhythm there that a straightforward attack on factory schooling couldn't do?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform the passage and articulate the sonic/comic mechanics, setting up Daniel to reframe it as structural critique and Edmund to push back on whether form or content is doing the moral work

questions.question: Daniel, you've said Stephen Blackpool is the only character in this novel who refuses the lie that the system is fixable. But Edmund would say — I think — that Stephen's paralysis is existential, not political. So when Stephen keeps saying 'tis a muddle' — is that a man naming a structural trap, or a man who simply cannot find his way out of himself?
questions.intent: Directly provoke the core disagreement between Daniel's systemic reading and Edmund's psychological one, using the muddle speeches as the battleground

questions.question: Edmund, you've argued the factory and the school are just a *stage* — that the real prison is one we build ourselves. But doesn't that create a problem with Rachael? Because when she screams 'He's down there! Down there!' — she's not screaming at a failure of character. She's screaming at a hole in the ground that the system left open. How do you hold your reading against that moment?
questions.intent: Put Edmund's psychological thesis under maximum pressure using the most viscerally physical passage in the novel — the shaft that kills Stephen — and force him to either defend or complicate his position

questions.question: Oliver, you've said Rachael's hysteria at the shaft could be dismissed as melodrama — but that in performance it becomes the only sane response to industrial horror. Daniel thinks it's the logical endpoint of a system that was always going to claim Stephen. Edmund thinks it's grief in its purest, most individual form. Can all three of those things be true at once, or does one of them have to give?
questions.intent: Force a three-way synthesis or collision on the novel's most emotionally loaded passage, and let each expert defend why their interpretive frame isn't just compatible but *necessary*

questions.question: Daniel, last one — and I want you to be honest here. Dickens was enormously popular. He was entertainment. Oliver says that's precisely *how* the moral trap works — you can't stop reading, so you can't escape feeling the muddle. But does a novel this entertaining, this full of grotesques and comic timing, actually *challenge* the system — or does it let the Victorian reader feel the outrage and then go home satisfied?
questions.intent: Push Daniel on whether Dickens's formal pleasures defuse rather than amplify his radicalism — a question that also challenges Oliver's strongest take and gives Edmund an opening to argue the novel's real value is timeless rather than political

steering_notes: The central fault line is structural critique (Daniel) vs. psychological interiority (Edmund) vs. formal and performative power (Oliver). Don't let the segment settle into each expert presenting their lane — push them into each other's territory. Oliver's readings should be treated as evidence both Daniel and Edmund want to claim for their own argument. The muddle speeches and the shaft scene are the two passages that can carry the most weight; return to them if the conversation goes abstract. Keep Edmund from retreating into 'timeless human nature' without being challenged — that's the position most likely to feel like a dodge on radio. Let Oliver read aloud at least once; it changes the register of the conversation in a useful way.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver says the pianoforte legs passage is comedy and music; Daniel says it's Dickens explicitly equating the factory and the schoolroom as institutions — these are not incompatible but they're also not the same claim, and forcing the distinction produces good radio

Daniel argues Stephen's 'muddle' is radical lucidity and structural diagnosis; Edmund argues it's the paralysis of goodness trapped in circumstance — this is the sharpest direct contradiction in the pre-interviews and should be the segment's centrepiece

Edmund's claim that Mrs. Gradgrind's suffering comes from personal vacancy rather than social position directly contradicts Oliver's reading of her as a figure of emotional suffocation produced by the system — worth surfacing if there's time

Oliver's strongest take — that Dickens traps the reader in the same moral cage as the characters through pleasure — is a bridge between Daniel's systemic reading and Edmund's psychological one, and could be used to de-escalate or reframe if the disagreement becomes unproductive

questions.question: Edmund, you've said Dickens isn't really attacking capitalism — he's attacking rationalism as a philosophy. But Daniel, I suspect, would say that's letting the factory owners off the hook. So let me put it to you directly: when those workers are sneaking off to read stories in the library, is that a spiritual act or a political one?
questions.intent: Open the central disagreement between Edmund and Daniel — individual conscience vs. systemic critique — and let it run

questions.question: Daniel, you want to read the parenthetical in c7:p66 — 'though not to him, for he saw nothing of it' — as Dickens saying the system literally cannot perceive what defeats it. But isn't there a risk that reading turns Gradgrind into a symbol and stops him being a person? Oliver thinks Dickens is performing his moral vision, not arguing it. Does it matter?
questions.intent: Get Daniel and Oliver into productive friction over whether Dickens's method is rhetorical performance or political anatomy — and force the question of whether Gradgrind earns any sympathy

questions.question: Oliver, you've called Sissy the novel's secret dramatic engine — she doesn't argue, she just persists. Can you read us c7:p2, the 'To do unto others' moment? And then tell me: is that Dickens being sentimental, or is he doing something more cunning than it looks?
questions.intent: Get the passage read aloud — let the room hear it — then use it to surface the disagreement about whether Sissy is redemptive figure, political symbol, or something stranger

questions.question: Daniel, you said something in our chat beforehand that I want to push on: that the novel is much colder than it looks. Edmund thinks the ending is basically about grace — something in Sissy that transcends the system. You think Gradgrind learns nothing about his own complicity, just that his method failed. If you're right, is this a hopeful book at all?
questions.intent: Force the sharpest disagreement of the segment — Edmund's 'conversion of heart' vs Daniel's 'cold defeat' — and see if Oliver can mediate or complicate

questions.question: Last one, and it's a bit of a trap — so I'm asking you, Oliver, because you'll enjoy it. Dickens keeps being claimed by everyone: Edmund says he's a conservative who trusts individual conscience, Daniel says he's exposing class power dressed as reason, and you're saying the whole argument lives in the rhythm of the prose. Can all three of those be true at once? Or does one of them have to give?
questions.intent: Force a synthesis or a decisive fracture — get each expert to commit to their strongest claim before the segment closes

steering_notes: The core tension to keep alive throughout is Edmund's 'spiritual indestructibility' reading vs Daniel's 'political cold water' reading, with Oliver as a kind of referee who thinks both are missing the point because the argument lives in the performance of the prose. Don't let Edmund and Daniel talk past each other through abstraction — pull them back to the specific passages whenever it goes too philosophical. The c7:p66 parenthetical and the c7:p2 golden rule moment are the two passages most likely to generate real heat. Push for readings aloud where possible — Oliver especially will respond well to this. Watch out for Daniel slipping into lecture mode on class; redirect him to the text.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund claims the workers in the library are asserting an individual, even religious, need for stories — Daniel explicitly argues they are resisting a system that starves them of meaning. These are irreconcilable and should be put head to head on c6:p4.

Oliver insists Gradgrind's blindness in c7:p66 is comic and ironic — Dickens lets us laugh at him. Daniel insists it's cold and structural. Edmund thinks it's about the limits of rationalism as a life philosophy. All three are reading the same parenthetical completely differently — worth pausing and making each of them say what that one clause is doing.

Daniel warns against reading Sissy as a redemptive figure for Louisa or Gradgrind. Edmund's entire closing argument is that she represents grace working through individual conscience. This is a direct collision that should be named explicitly.
